accepted_scope_caveats.label: honest_scope / no-dominance-frontier
accepted_scope_caveats.caveat: The claimed frontier is conditional on known unequal disjoint cliques, balanced unit Bernoulli assignment, correct unanimous exposure mapping, and bounded fixed schedules.
accepted_scope_caveats.bound_claim: The field-level frontier concerns this fixed-design clique family only; it does not claim arbitrary-graph, optimized-design, or variance-adaptive optimality.

source_verification_receipts.locator: p. 329 abstract; pp. 330-331, network-exposure and clustering setup
source_verification_receipts.verified_claim: The proceedings paper defines network exposure, computes exposure probabilities under graph cluster randomization, uses inverse-weighted HT estimation, and contrasts exponential degree dependence with restricted-growth variance control.
The preprint develops design-based minimax risk under arbitrary neighborhood interference through a conflict graph and gives upper and lower minimax-rate bounds for direct and global effects.
The preprint studies finite-sample treatment-effect confidence intervals for ordinary randomized experiments, closes an effective-sample-size gap, and states information-theoretic rate optimality.
The article shows that even structural assumptions permitting unbiased estimation under network interference need not ensure decreasing large-sample variance.
The article introduces randomized graph cluster randomization, motivated by extreme HT variance, and changes clustering to improve GATE estimation.
The preprint introduces a conflict-graph design, a modified HT estimator, spectral variance control, and asymptotically valid conservative intervals.
The paper uses between-class moduli for expected-length lower bounds and ordered moduli for constant-factor adaptive confidence procedures in a Gaussian model.
The paper derives finite-sample optimal confidence intervals and sharp efficiency bounds for linear functionals over convex regression classes under normal known-variance errors.
The preprint studies randomized fuzzy confidence intervals and states a minimum-maximum-expected-length result for a Bernoulli trial observation.
